turns.prompt_text: okay, I like to use the default terminal in Mac. I like to use Fish as well.
turns.response_html:
That is a fantastic combination. The macOS Terminal is solid and reliable, but Fish (Friendly Interactive Shell) is what really brings it to life. Most people stick with Zsh because it's the Mac default, but Fish is arguably the most "intelligent" shell out of the box.

Since you are already using them together, here are a few ways to level up that specific workflow:

1. The "Killer Features" of Fish

Unlike Bash or Zsh, Fish doesn’t require a massive configuration file (like a .zshrc) to feel modern. It comes with:

  • Autosuggestions: It suggests commands as you type based on your history. You just hit the Right Arrow or Ctrl+F to complete them.
  • Web-based Config: If you haven't tried it yet, run fish_config in your terminal. It opens a local web page where you can visually pick your theme and colors.
  • Syntax Highlighting: It catches typos before you even hit Enter—commands turn red if they are invalid and blue if they are correct.

2. Essential Utilities for Mac Terminal

To make the default Mac Terminal feel more powerful alongside Fish, consider these "drop-in" replacements for standard commands:

  • exa or eza: A modern replacement for ls. It uses colors and icons to make file listings much more readable.
  • bat: A replacement for cat that adds syntax highlighting and line numbers when you're peaking into files.
  • fzf (Fuzzy Finder): This is a game-changer. It integrates with Fish to let you search through your command history or files with lightning speed.

3. Quick Customization Tip: The Prompt

If you want a prompt that gives you more information (like what Git branch you're on) without manually coding it, you might like Starship. It’s a cross-shell prompt that works beautifully with Fish.

To install it via Homebrew:

brew install starship
echo "starship init fish | source" >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish

Would you like some help setting up specific Fish abbreviations (aliases) to speed up your most common tasks, or are you looking for ways to customize the visual theme of your Terminal?

eza is the modern, community-maintained successor to the older exa tool. It’s written in Rust and makes your file listings look beautiful with colors, Git integration, and icons.

Since you're using Fish on macOS, here is how to get it running and deeply integrated into your workflow.

1. Install eza

If you have Homebrew installed, run:

brew install eza

2. Add Icons (The "Nerd Font" Step)

eza can display icons for different file types (like a Python logo next to .py files). However, the default macOS fonts don't support these symbols.

  1. Install a Nerd Font: The easiest way is via Homebrew: 
    brew tap homebrew/cask-fonts
brew install --cask font-meslo-lg-nerd-font
  2. Update Terminal Settings: * Open Terminal Settings (Cmd + ,).
    • Go to Profiles > Text.
    • Click Change under Font and select MesloLGS Nerd Font.

3. Setting Up Fish Abbreviations

In Fish, we prefer abbreviations over traditional aliases. When you type an abbreviation and hit Space, it expands to the full command so you can see exactly what you're running.

Run these commands in your terminal to set them up permanently:

# Basic replacement for ls
abbr -a ls 'eza --icons'

# Long view: shows file sizes, headers, and git status
abbr -a ll 'eza -l --icons --git --header'

# Detailed view: includes hidden files
abbr -a la 'eza -la --icons --git --header'

# Tree view: see the directory structure
abbr -a lt 'eza --tree --icons'

4. Advanced "Power User" Setup

If you want eza to automatically sort folders first or show a color scale for file ages, you can create a more complex abbreviation in your config.fish file:

  1. Open your config: nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish
  2. Add this logic to make sure eza only runs if it's actually installed:
if type -q eza
    alias ls='eza --icons --group-directories-first'
    alias ll='eza -l --icons --git --group-directories-first'
    alias llt='eza 1 --tree --icons'
end

Why this is better for you:

  • Visual Hierarchy: Directories are grouped at the top, making navigation in your university or coding projects much faster.
  • Git Integration: In the ll view, you'll see a column showing which files are modified (M) or new (N) without needing to run git status.
  • Readability: It uses "human-readable" sizes (like 1.2K instead of 1224) by default.

turns.prompt_text: the command "lt" went away when I restarted fish
turns.response_html:
That happens because the abbr -a command only adds the abbreviation to your current session unless it's explicitly saved to your configuration file.

In Fish, to make an abbreviation "sticky" so it survives a restart, you have two options. Given your preference for a clean setup, I recommend Option 1.

Option 1: Add it to your Config File (Recommended)

This is the most reliable way to ensure your aliases and abbreviations are always there.

  1. Open your Fish config file: 
    nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish
  2. Scroll to the bottom and paste these lines: 
    # eza abbreviations
abbr -a ls 'eza --icons'
abbr -a ll 'eza -l --icons --git --header'
abbr -a la 'eza -la --icons --git --header'
abbr -a lt 'eza --tree --icons'
  3. Press Ctrl+O, Enter (to save), and Ctrl+X (to exit).
  4. Restart your terminal or run source ~/.config/fish/config.fish.

Option 2: The "Universal" Command

Fish has a feature called Universal Variables. If you run the command with the -U flag, Fish will remember it across all future sessions without you having to touch a config file.

Run this in your terminal once:

abbr -a -U lt 'eza --tree --icons'

A Quick Pro-Tip for lt

Since you're using lt for a tree view, sometimes listing every file in a deep project (like a node_modules folder or a complex math project) can get messy. You can limit the depth by typing: lt --level 2

Now that lt is permanent, would you like to set up bat next? It’s essentially "eza for file contents"—it adds syntax highlighting and line numbers when you view code or text files.

bat is essentially cat on steroids. It gives you syntax highlighting, line numbers, and even shows you Git modifications (like eza does) directly in the sidebar while you're reading a file.

1. Install bat

Using Homebrew:

brew install bat

2. Set Up the "Stickiness"

Just like we did with eza, let's add this to your config.fish so it becomes your new default way of looking at files.

  1. Open your config: nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish
  2. Add these lines to the bottom: 
    # bat abbreviation
abbr -a cat 'bat'
    Note: By using cat as the abbreviation, every time you type cat and hit space, it will expand to bat. This helps you unlearn the habit of using the basic tool.

3. Change the Visual Theme

bat comes with several themes. You can see them all by running:

bat --list-themes

If you find one you like (for example, "Nord" or "Dracula"), you can set it permanently in your Fish config by adding this line:

set -x BAT_THEME "Dracula"

4. Use Case: Why this helps you

Since you're studying Math Education and Computer Science, you'll likely be looking at a lot of code or LaTeX files.

  • For CS: Running cat script.py will now show you a beautifully highlighted Python script.
  • For Math: If you view a .tex file, bat will highlight the LaTeX syntax, making it much easier to spot a missing bracket or command.

One Last "Secret" Trick:

If you want to view a file but it’s huge and you don’t want to scroll, you can pipe eza into bat. Try this:

lt | bat

It will take your directory tree and put it inside a bat window where you can scroll through it using your arrow keys.

turns.prompt_text: Wait, let's add an easy way to access and modify the fish config file, and an easy way to update it
turns.response_html:
That is a pro-move. Manually typing out the full path to the config file every time is exactly the kind of friction that stops you from refining your setup.

Let’s add two abbreviations to your config.fish file: one to edit it and one to reload it (so changes take effect immediately without restarting the terminal).

1. The Setup

Open your config one last time the "hard" way: nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish

Add these two lines to your list of abbreviations:

# Fast config management
abbr -a fishconf 'nano ~/.config/fish/config.fish'
abbr -a fishup 'source ~/.config/fish/config.fish'

2. How to use them

  • fishconf: This will instantly open your configuration in Nano. (If you eventually switch to a different editor like VS Code, you can just change nano to code in that line later).
  • fishup: After you save and exit the editor, type this to "refresh" Fish. It’s much faster than closing and reopening the window.

3. A "Mnemonic" Bonus

Since you like short, intuitive commands (like lt and la), some Fish users also like to group their "system" shortcuts. You could also use:

  • conf for fishconf
  • reload for fishup

Summary of your new toolkit:

CommandWhat it does
ls / ll / ltBeautiful file listings via eza.
catHighlighted file contents via bat.
fishconfOpens your settings for a quick tweak.
fishupMakes your new settings live instantly.

Since you're now a "power editor" of your own config, would you like to see how to add your current Git branch to your prompt so you always know which version of a project you're working on?

Once you’ve added starship init fish | source to your config.fish, Starship works mostly "in the background"—it just makes your prompt smarter. However, the real magic is in how it reacts to your environment.

Here is how to use it and customize it to fit your style.

1. Understanding the Symbols

Starship is context-aware. You don't "run" Starship; it simply tells you what's happening based on where you are:

  • The Git Branch: If you are in a folder with a .git repo, it will show a branch symbol (usually ) and the name (e.g., main).
  • The Git Status: It uses symbols like + for new files, ! for modified files, and ✘ for deleted files.
  • The Language: If you are working on a project for your CS degree, it will detect files like package.json (Node.js), requirements.txt (Python), or Cargo.toml (Rust) and show the version of that language you are currently using.

2. Customizing the Look

If you don't like the default look, you can change everything via a single file. Unlike Fish, which uses .fish files, Starship uses a TOML file.

  1. Create the config directory: 
    mkdir -p ~/.config
  2. Create the config file: 
    nano ~/.config/starship.toml

3. Try a Preset

If you want to quickly change the vibe, you can paste one of these "recipes" into your starship.toml:

The "Minimalist" (Very clean):

# Get a simple, clean prompt
format = '$directory$git_branch$git_status$character'

[directory]
style = "bold blue"

[character]
success_symbol = "[➜](bold green)"
error_symbol = "[➜](bold red)"

The "Powerline" (Bold blocks of color): Starship has built-in presets you can explore. To see them, run:

starship preset --list

To apply one (e.g., the "nerd-font-symbols" preset), run:

starship preset nerd-font-symbols -o ~/.config/starship.toml

4. How to "Use" it for Troubleshooting

One of the best "hidden" features is the Command Duration. If you run a command that takes a long time (like a complex math simulation or a large code compile), Starship will automatically show you exactly how long it took (e.g., 2s) right next to the prompt once it finishes.
